{"command": "cd "$WORKSPACE_DIR"; cat > build/p7_modlow.py <<'PYEOF'
# ================= 6. MODERATE =================
doc.add_page_break()
H1("Moderate-Severity Issues", "6")
P("The issues below either leave a requirement unverified or rest on an analytical basis that is unsound or unsupported. None is presently established as a violation on the documents in the record; several would convert to High or Critical once the municipal file is produced. They should be closed out during the Inspection Period.")

H2("6.1  M-1 — Bicycle parking was never addressed")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-42(d) requires that \"All mixed-use developments and all commercial developments providing fifty (50) or more vehicular parking spaces shall provide bicycle parking at a ratio of one (1) bicycle parking space per twenty (20) vehicular parking spaces, with a minimum of four (4) bicycle spaces,\" with racks that support the frame upright, located within 100 feet of the main building entrance and identified by signage. Applying the 187 spaces counted by the Survey gives **9.35, rounded to 10 spaces**. The Report does not mention bicycle parking, and the Survey does not identify any racks. This is a mandatory standard in the same section the Report cites, and the property is both a mixed-use development and a commercial development with more than 50 spaces, so the requirement is engaged twice over.")
label_par("Action.", "Confirm whether bicycle parking exists; if not, install 10 spaces within 100 feet of the Building A main entrance with signage, or include the deficiency in the cure package and the Report correction.")

H2("6.2  M-2 — Accessible parking: the count is adequate, the specification is unverified")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-42(e) requires, for a lot with 151 to 200 spaces, a minimum of **6 accessible spaces including 1 van-accessible space**; van-accessible spaces must be at least 11 feet wide with an adjacent 5-foot access aisle, and accessible spaces must be on the shortest accessible route to the entrance. The Survey counts \"8 ADA-accessible spaces located near the main entrance to Building A,\" so the numerical requirement is met with a margin. The Report asserts compliance generically — \"Accessible parking spaces are provided in accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act and the New Jersey Barrier Free Subcode, as reflected in the building permit records\" — without recording the width, aisle, signage or route of any space.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain a striping and signage plan or an accessibility survey confirming at least one van-accessible space of the specified dimensions.")

H2("6.3  M-3 — The 28-foot rear-yard figure cannot be reconciled with the survey's own geometry")
label_par("Finding.", "The Survey attributes the 28.0-foot rear yard to **Building A**, \"measured ... from the north face of Building A to the north property line,\" and the Report adopts that attribution. The geometry does not close. Building A has a 14,000 SF footprint; the Report gives its Crescent Boulevard frontage as approximately 120 linear feet, which implies a depth of about 116.7 feet. The Report and the Survey both give the front yard as 22.0 feet and the lot depth as 587.0 feet. On those figures Building A's north face stands roughly 139 feet from the Crescent Boulevard line and roughly **448 feet** from the north property line — not 28 feet.")
P("The 28.0-foot measurement is far more plausibly a measurement of **Building B**, which the Survey places \"in the northern portion of the site, behind and to the north of Building A.\" If that is so, Building B's north face is 28 feet from the R-4 boundary and its 25-foot-deep loading apron extends to within about 3 feet of it. That would place the entire loading operation inside the 35-foot enhanced rear setback, and directly opposite R-4 residences across the boundary — which is consistent with H-2 and gives that issue a larger footprint than the Report suggests.")
P("This does not soften C-1. Whichever building stands 28 feet from the north line, the measured setback is 7 feet short of the 35-foot requirement. What it changes is which structure requires relief, and how much of the site is affected. It also means the Report's statement that \"The rear yard setback of 28 feet for Building A exceeds the applicable 25-foot minimum\" describes a condition that cannot exist on the survey's own dimensions.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain a corrected setback exhibit from Cartwright Surveying Associates identifying the rear setback for each building separately, together with the dimension from each building to the nearest point of the north property line.")

H2("6.4  M-4 — The character of the north yard is unresolved, and it affects the standard applied")
label_par("Finding.", "The Survey's boundary description at Section 2 states that the property is bounded \"on the north by **Lots 5 and 6, Block 413 (R-4 Residential zone)**\" and identifies no street along that line; the metes and bounds description runs the north line between the northeast and northwest corners without reference to Elm Terrace. But Sections 6 and 9 of the same Survey identify **Elm Terrace**, a 40-foot publicly dedicated right-of-way, at the rear of the site, with Curb Cut No. 3 taken from it at the northwest corner. The Report follows neither description consistently: Section 3.3 says the property has \"frontage on both Crescent Boulevard to the south and Elm Terrace to the north (rear),\" while Section IV.C says the north boundary \"adjoins Elm Terrace, beyond which lies the R-4 Residential District.\"")
P("Two characterisations are available, and they produce different obligations. If the north yard is a **rear yard abutting a residential zone**, the 35-foot enhanced setback and the prohibition on parking, loading and structures within it both apply (C-1), as does the 15-foot buffer (H-1). If the north line is a **street frontage on Elm Terrace**, then the 20-foot front yard standard in § 245-18(h)(1) applies — that subsection provides that on a corner lot each street frontage is deemed a front yard, and a lot with frontage on two streets presents the analogous question — and § 245-42(g)(4) prohibits loading spaces \"within any required front yard setback area.\" Whichever characterisation is correct, the loading area in the north yard fails; but the relief required differs, and the buffer obligation may differ as well.")
label_par("Action.", "Request a written determination from the Zoning Officer on the character of the north yard. This is the single cheapest step available to fix the applicable standard, and it should precede any application.")

H2("6.5  M-5 — The monument sign's other requirements were never tested")
label_par("Finding.", "Beyond height and area (C-6), § 245-50 imposes further requirements on a B-3 monument sign, none of which the Report addresses: a minimum **5-foot setback from any property line**, exclusion from any sight triangle and from any required landscaped buffer (§ 245-50(c)(1)(iv)); a base of brick, natural stone, cast stone or architectural precast concrete, with wood and unfinished concrete block prohibited (§ 245-50(c)(1)(v)); and illumination only by shielded external fixtures or reverse-channel letters with an opaque cabinet (§ 245-50(c)(1)(vi)). The Survey places the sign \"immediately east of the primary curb cut (Curb Cut No. 1),\" which makes the sight-triangle requirement a live question rather than a formality. Separately, the Report states that the sign \"was permitted under the building permit records reviewed\"; § 245-50 requires a **sign permit** from the Construction Official for all signs not exempt under § 245-50(h), which is a different instrument from a building permit.")
label_par("Action.", "Test each requirement and obtain the sign permit file. The result may add to the cure cost or may supply a basis to contest the C-6 deficiency.")

H2("6.6  M-6 — Building B's wall-sign frontage basis is unsupported and the facade is misdescribed")
label_par("Finding.", "The Report measures Building B's wall-sign allowance against \"a primary frontage facing the internal parking lot of approximately **100 linear feet**\" (100 × 1.5 = 150 SF). No such dimension appears in the Survey or anywhere else in the record, and the Survey records the sign on the \"south-facing (parking lot side) facade\" whereas the Report places it on the \"west façade.\" More fundamentally, § 245-50(a) defines \"building frontage\" as \"the linear measurement of the building wall **facing a public street**\" and, for buildings not facing a public street, as \"the linear measurement of the building wall **containing the primary entrance**.\" Building B does not face a public street on the side in question, so the parking-lot wall is the wrong measure.")
P("The 32 SF sign will very likely comply on any plausible frontage — a frontage as short as 25 feet would still permit 37.5 SF — so we do not rank this as a violation. It is ranked as Moderate because the Report has arrived at a compliance conclusion through an invented dimension and a misidentified facade, which is the same pattern of reasoning that produced C-6 and materially affects the weight the Buyer can place on the signage section.")
label_par("Action.", "Measure Building B's frontage to the wall containing its primary entrance and restate the allowance.")

H2("6.7  M-7 — Rooftop mechanical equipment height was not tested, and the headroom is one foot")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-18(d) limits height to 45 feet or 3 stories, whichever is less, and permits rooftop mechanical equipment, penthouses and stairway bulkheads to exceed the limit by not more than **10 feet**, provided they are set back from the building perimeter by at least their own height above the roofline and occupy not more than **20% of the total roof area**. The Survey measures Building A at \"44 feet, measured from average finished grade at the building perimeter to the highest point of the roof structure (**parapet cap**),\" and records that \"rooftop mechanical equipment [was] observed behind the parapet.\" The measurement therefore excludes the equipment. With only one foot of headroom to the 45-foot limit, any unit projecting more than a foot above the parapet engages the appurtenance allowance, whose two conditions have not been tested.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain elevations or an as-built survey showing the height of the rooftop equipment above the parapet, its setback from the perimeter, and the roof area it occupies. Although the building satisfies the 3-story limb, the footage limit applies independently.")

H2("6.8  M-8 — Floodplain, drainage easement and stormwater facilities in the rear yard")
label_par("Finding.", "The Survey records that approximately **0.3 acres (13,068 SF)** of the northeast corner lies within FEMA Flood Zone AE with a base flood elevation of 42.0 feet NAVD88, extending about 75 feet along the north boundary and 175 feet along the east boundary, and that the area is \"covered by turf grass and a portion of the rear parking area.\" It records a **15-foot drainage easement** in the same northeast corner in favour of the Essex County Flood Control and Drainage Authority, overlapping the flood zone. The ESA confirms the area is at lower grade with hydric soil indicators and sediment deposits on pavement near the Elm Terrace curb cut.")
P("Section 245-18(h)(3) permits only landscaping and **stormwater management facilities expressly approved by the Planning Board** within the enhanced rear yard, and § 245-18(i) prohibits stormwater facilities within the landscaped buffer — a tension that must be resolved by design rather than assumed. The Report disclaims flood matters (Section 2.3(3) and Section X), which is defensible as a matter of scope, but its Recommendation 2 on \"significant remaining development capacity\" does not account for the fact that roughly 13,068 SF is both floodplain and easement-burdened, or that rear parking appears to sit within the prohibited rear-yard zone.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain the site plan and any stormwater approval; confirm whether any stormwater facility lies within the enhanced rear yard or the buffer, and whether it was expressly approved by the Planning Board. Have a design professional confirm the floodplain and flood-hazard status against the current effective FIRM panel (see L-2).")

H2("6.9  M-9 — No certificate of compliance or zoning permit is established")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-60(a) prohibits construction or a change of use without a zoning permit, and § 245-60(b) prohibits occupancy until the Zoning Officer issues a **certificate of compliance** confirming conformity with Chapter 245 \"including **all conditions of any variance approval, conditional use approval, or site plan approval**,\" and provides that the Zoning Officer \"shall not issue a certificate of compliance until all conditions of approval have been satisfied.\" The Report relies throughout on \"Certificate of Occupancy records\" — a different instrument, which is not evidence of zoning compliance — and does not identify any record by date or number. If the buffer condition, the loading screening condition and the conditions of a conditional use were unsatisfied, no valid certificate of compliance ought to have issued for Building B.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain the complete zoning permit and certificate of compliance file for both buildings under § 245-60(c). This is the single most probative document request in the matter.")

H2("6.10  M-10 — The annual hazardous-materials certification has never been evidenced")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-15(c)(3)(c) does not merely prohibit the storage of hazardous materials; it requires that \"The applicant shall provide a **certification to the Planning Board, at the time of application and annually thereafter**, that no hazardous materials are stored on-site.\" Because no conditional use application was ever made (C-3), no baseline certification exists, and no annual certification has been filed. The Report does not mention the obligation. The Report's observation that the consultant is \"not aware\" of any storage is not a certification and does not discharge it. Given the ESA's REC-1 and its recommendation for a Phase II including sub-slab vapour sampling, any certification should be given only after that work is complete, so that it can be given accurately.")
label_par("Action.", "Include the certification obligation in the conditional use application and align its timing with the Phase II investigation recommended by Greystone.")

# ================= 7. LOW =================
H1("Low-Severity Issues — Documentation Integrity and Residual Defects", "7")
P("These matters do not by themselves change the compliance result, but each impedes audit or reliance, and each should be corrected before Closing so that the instruments the parties are relying on can be shown to be the same instruments.")

H2("7.1  L-1 — Document control: the record cites three different surveyor licence numbers and conflicting project numbers")
mktable(
    ["Identifier", "Report [Report]", "Survey [Survey]", "PSA [PSA]", "Remark"],
    [
        ["Surveyor licence no. (Thomas Cartwright, PLS)", "24GS05127", "38742", "28GS04117900", "**Three different numbers** for the same professional"],
        ["Survey drawing / job no.", "not cited", "CS-2025-0047 (Sheet 1 of 2)", "CSA-2025-1148", "**Two different numbers**"],
        ["ESA project no.", "not cited", "not cited", "GE-2025-0441", "ESA itself reads **GEC-2025-0147**"],
        ["Report project no.", "PLA-2025-0087", "—", "—", "Consistent"],
    ],
    [Inches(1.70), Inches(1.10), Inches(1.34), Inches(1.10), Inches(1.26)],
    align=["l", "c", "c", "c", "l"], font=7.8, hdr_font=8.0)
spacer(2)
P("Individually these are clerical. Cumulatively they matter, because the Buyer must be able to demonstrate under § 8.2(a) and § 8.3(a) that the survey it has reviewed and on which it will object is the survey delivered under the Agreement, and because two of the identifiers (the ESA project number and the survey licence number) appear in the Agreement itself. The discrepancies should be corrected by amendment or by a Closing certificate identifying the conformed documents.")
H2("7.2  L-2 — Two different FIRM panels are cited for the same flood zone")
P("The Survey (Section 8) cites FIRM Panel No. **34013C0042F**, effective December 4, 2020. The ESA (Sections 4 and 5.4) cites FIRM Panel No. **34013C0038J**, effective June 4, 2021. Both state a base flood elevation of 42.0 feet NAVD88 and both place approximately 0.3 acres in Zone AE, so the substance agrees; but only one panel can be current, and the floodplain analysis for any future application must rest on the effective panel. The discrepancy should be resolved through FEMA's map service or the Borough.")
H2("7.3  L-3 — The PSA recites a 12-foot variance where the resolution grants 18 feet")
P("PSA § 5.3(f) represents that the variance authorises \"a reduced east side yard setback of **twelve feet (12')** for Building B (where twenty-five feet (25') is otherwise required).\" The resolution grants **eighteen (18) feet** — in recital 8, recital 9, the operative grant in Section 3, and the transferability clause in Section 4. The Report and the Survey both state 18 feet. The 12-foot recital is unsupported and understates the approved relief by six feet; it also misdescribes the as-built margin, which is 1 foot against 18 feet but would appear to be 7 feet against 12 feet. Because § 5.3 survives for 24 months, the recital should be corrected by amendment before Closing rather than left to be argued about later.")
H2("7.4  L-4 — Building A programme conflict: residential upper floors in the variance recital, office as built")
P("Recital 5 of the resolution describes the approved programme as Building A \"contain[ing] ground-floor retail space with **residential dwelling units on the upper two floors**.\" The Report, the Survey and the ESA all describe the second and third floors as **professional office** (28,000 SF), and the ESA observed professional office tenants in occupation. Two explanations are possible: the development as built departed from the programme on which the variance was granted, or the recital recorded an intention that changed with approval. The distinction is worth resolving because the Board may take it into account on the § 4 confirmation application (C-4), and because if residential units had been built the parking requirement would have been 1.5 spaces per dwelling unit under § 245-42(b), with the unit count unknown, so the Report's 169-space computation would require revision. The use itself is permitted either way under § 245-15(a)(6). We carry the approved site plan as a document request.")
H2("7.5  L-5 — Residual citation and description defects")
BUL("Recital 4 of the resolution cites \"§ 245-16\" for the B-3 height standard; the ordinance excerpts place the bulk standards at § 245-18. This may reflect a renumbering, but the discrepancy should be noted if the resolution is relied on.")
BUL("The Report describes Building B as \"located to the north and east of Building A, toward the eastern portion of the property\"; the Survey places it \"in the northern portion of the site, behind and to the north of Building A.\"")
BUL("The Report computes building coverage from building footprints alone. Section 245-18(e) requires covered porches, porte-cochères and canopies to be included. At 17.77% against a 35% maximum the margin is wide and the omission is unlikely to be material, but the metric should be built on the stated basis.")
BUL("The Report places the Building B wall sign on the \"west façade\"; the Survey records it on the \"south-facing (parking lot side) facade.\"")
BUL("Section 2.2 of the Report lists six categories of materials reviewed, including building permit records, Certificate of Occupancy records and the tax map, but identifies none of them by date, number or issuer, which makes independent verification impossible.")
BUL("Recommendation 2 of the Report discusses \"significant remaining development capacity\" without reference to the east side yard constraint (C-4), the loading and buffer constraints (H-1, H-2, H-3), or the floodplain and easement constraints in the northeast corner (M-8). The capacity conclusion is therefore optimistic in a way that matters to a Buyer underwriting an expansion.")
PYEOF
python3 -c "print('p7 ok')""}

label_par("Action.", "Obtain a corrected setback exhibit from Cartwright Surveying Associates identifying the rear setback for each building separately, together with the dimension from each building to the nearest point of the north property line.")

H2("6.4  M-4 — The character of the north yard is unresolved, and it affects the standard applied")
label_par("Finding.", "The Survey's boundary description at Section 2 states that the property is bounded \"on the north by **Lots 5 and 6, Block 413 (R-4 Residential zone)**\" and identifies no street along that line; the metes and bounds description runs the north line between the northeast and northwest corners without reference to Elm Terrace. But Sections 6 and 9 of the same Survey identify **Elm Terrace**, a 40-foot publicly dedicated right-of-way, at the rear of the site, with Curb Cut No. 3 taken from it at the northwest corner. The Report follows neither description consistently: Section 3.3 says the property has \"frontage on both Crescent Boulevard to the south and Elm Terrace to the north (rear),\" while Section IV.C says the north boundary \"adjoins Elm Terrace, beyond which lies the R-4 Residential District.\"")
P("Two characterisations are available, and they produce different obligations. If the north yard is a **rear yard abutting a residential zone**, the 35-foot enhanced setback and the prohibition on parking, loading and structures within it both apply (C-1), as does the 15-foot buffer (H-1). If the north line is a **street frontage on Elm Terrace**, then the 20-foot front yard standard in § 245-18(h)(1) applies — that subsection provides that on a corner lot each street frontage is deemed a front yard, and a lot with frontage on two streets presents the analogous question — and § 245-42(g)(4) prohibits loading spaces \"within any required front yard setback area.\" Whichever characterisation is correct, the loading area in the north yard fails; but the relief required differs, and the buffer obligation may differ as well.")
label_par("Action.", "Request a written determination from the Zoning Officer on the character of the north yard. This is the single cheapest step available to fix the applicable standard, and it should precede any application.")

H2("6.5  M-5 — The monument sign's other requirements were never tested")
label_par("Finding.", "Beyond height and area (C-6), § 245-50 imposes further requirements on a B-3 monument sign, none of which the Report addresses: a minimum **5-foot setback from any property line**, exclusion from any sight triangle and from any required landscaped buffer (§ 245-50(c)(1)(iv)); a base of brick, natural stone, cast stone or architectural precast concrete, with wood and unfinished concrete block prohibited (§ 245-50(c)(1)(v)); and illumination only by shielded external fixtures or reverse-channel letters with an opaque cabinet (§ 245-50(c)(1)(vi)). The Survey places the sign \"immediately east of the primary curb cut (Curb Cut No. 1),\" which makes the sight-triangle requirement a live question rather than a formality. Separately, the Report states that the sign \"was permitted under the building permit records reviewed\"; § 245-50 requires a **sign permit** from the Construction Official for all signs not exempt under § 245-50(h), which is a different instrument from a building permit.")
label_par("Action.", "Test each requirement and obtain the sign permit file. The result may add to the cure cost or may supply a basis to contest the C-6 deficiency.")

H2("6.6  M-6 — Building B's wall-sign frontage basis is unsupported and the facade is misdescribed")
label_par("Finding.", "The Report measures Building B's wall-sign allowance against \"a primary frontage facing the internal parking lot of approximately **100 linear feet**\" (100 × 1.5 = 150 SF). No such dimension appears in the Survey or anywhere else in the record, and the Survey records the sign on the \"south-facing (parking lot side) facade\" whereas the Report places it on the \"west façade.\" More fundamentally, § 245-50(a) defines \"building frontage\" as \"the linear measurement of the building wall **facing a public street**\" and, for buildings not facing a public street, as \"the linear measurement of the building wall **containing the primary entrance**.\" Building B does not face a public street on the side in question, so the parking-lot wall is the wrong measure.")
P("The 32 SF sign will very likely comply on any plausible frontage — a frontage as short as 25 feet would still permit 37.5 SF — so we do not rank this as a violation. label_par("Action.", "Measure Building B's frontage to the wall containing its primary entrance and restate the allowance.")

H2("6.7  M-7 — Rooftop mechanical equipment height was not tested, and the headroom is one foot")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-18(d) limits height to 45 feet or 3 stories, whichever is less, and permits rooftop mechanical equipment, penthouses and stairway bulkheads to exceed the limit by not more than **10 feet**, provided they are set back from the building perimeter by at least their own height above the roofline and occupy not more than **20% of the total roof area**. The Survey measures Building A at \"44 feet, measured from average finished grade at the building perimeter to the highest point of the roof structure (**parapet cap**),\" and records that \"rooftop mechanical equipment [was] observed behind the parapet.\" The measurement therefore excludes the equipment. With only one foot of headroom to the 45-foot limit, any unit projecting more than a foot above the parapet engages the appurtenance allowance, whose two conditions have not been tested.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain elevations or an as-built survey showing the height of the rooftop equipment above the parapet, its setback from the perimeter, and the roof area it occupies. Although the building satisfies the 3-story limb, the footage limit applies independently.")

H2("6.8  M-8 — Floodplain, drainage easement and stormwater facilities in the rear yard")
label_par("Finding.", "The Survey records that approximately **0.3 acres (13,068 SF)** of the northeast corner lies within FEMA Flood Zone AE with a base flood elevation of 42.0 feet NAVD88, extending about 75 feet along the north boundary and 175 feet along the east boundary, and that the area is \"covered by turf grass and a portion of the rear parking area.\" It records a **15-foot drainage easement** in the same northeast corner in favour of the Essex County Flood Control and Drainage Authority, overlapping the flood zone. P("Section 245-18(h)(3) permits only landscaping and **stormwater management facilities expressly approved by the Planning Board** within the enhanced rear yard, and § 245-18(i) prohibits stormwater facilities within the landscaped buffer — a tension that must be resolved by design rather than assumed. label_par("Action.", "Obtain the site plan and any stormwater approval; confirm whether any stormwater facility lies within the enhanced rear yard or the buffer, and whether it was expressly approved by the Planning Board. Have a design professional confirm the floodplain and flood-hazard status against the current effective FIRM panel (see L-2).")

H2("6.9  M-9 — No certificate of compliance or zoning permit is established")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-60(a) prohibits construction or a change of use without a zoning permit, and § 245-60(b) prohibits occupancy until the Zoning Officer issues a **certificate of compliance** confirming conformity with Chapter 245 \"including **all conditions of any variance approval, conditional use approval, or site plan approval**,\" and provides that the Zoning Officer \"shall not issue a certificate of compliance until all conditions of approval have been satisfied.\" The Report relies throughout on \"Certificate of Occupancy records\" — a different instrument, which is not evidence of zoning compliance — and does not identify any record by date or number. If the buffer condition, the loading screening condition and the conditions of a conditional use were unsatisfied, no valid certificate of compliance ought to have issued for Building B.")
label_par("Action.", "Obtain the complete zoning permit and certificate of compliance file for both buildings under § 245-60(c). This is the single most probative document request in the matter.")

H2("6.10  M-10 — The annual hazardous-materials certification has never been evidenced")
label_par("Finding.", "Section 245-15(c)(3)(c) does not merely prohibit the storage of hazardous materials; it requires that \"The applicant shall provide a **certification to the Planning Board, at the time of application and annually thereafter**, that no hazardous materials are stored on-site.\" Because no conditional use application was ever made (C-3), no baseline certification exists, and no annual certification has been filed. label_par("Action.", "Include the certification obligation in the conditional use application and align its timing with the Phase II investigation recommended by Greystone.")

1. Executive Summary
Bottom line. The Zoning Compliance Report concludes that the property is in
compliance with all applicable bulk, use, parking, and sign regulations of the B-3
Mixed-Use Business District, subject only to the 2013 variance. That conclusion is not
supported by the documents the Report purports to rely on. Our review identifies six
critical issues, several of which are outright non-compliance that the Report either
misstates affirmatively or does not address at all.
Two of the six critical issues arise from the same defect of method: the Report
transcribes the ordinance's base standards and omits the enhanced standards that
apply because the property abuts an R-4 Residential zone on its north and east
boundaries. The Report correctly carries forward the enhanced 25-foot side yard
standard for the east boundary, but drops the parallel enhanced 35-foot rear yard
standard for the north boundary — a 7-foot deficiency that the Report certifies as
compliant. A related error appears in the sign analysis, where the Report states the B-3

standard correctly and then applies the adjoining B-2 district's more permissive
monument sign standards, concealing a 2-foot height overage and a 50% area overage.
The remaining critical issues go to the property's use entitlements and to the durability
of the only relief it holds. The warehouse/flex use occupies 30.58% of total gross floor
area against a conditional-use ceiling of 25% — the Report's stated 24% is an
arithmetic error. The warehouse/flex use also has no Planning Board conditional
use approval, an approval the variance resolution expressly requires as a separate
and additional act, and which the Report asserts is unnecessary. And the 2013
variance, on which the Report's entire compliance conclusion depends, is personal to
the Seller and expires automatically on transfer unless a successor files a
confirmation application within 90 days — a term the Report does not mention
anywhere.

 In practical terms: the property does not hold the land use approvals that its physical condition
 requires, and the one approval it does hold will not survive this sale in its current form.
 Separately, the Report is addressed to the Seller and, by its own confidentiality notice, may not be
 relied upon by "any prospective purchaser." The Buyer therefore holds a document that is wrong
 in material respects and which it has no legal right to rely upon.


Summary of findings. Twenty-eight issues are identified. Six are Critical, seven High,
ten Moderate and five Low. The distribution is set out below and each issue is analysed
in Sections 4 to 7.

You have asked us to review the Seller's Zoning Compliance Report and to test its
conclusions against the source documents on which it relies. This memorandum is
prepared on behalf of the Buyer in support of three decisions reserved to the Buyer
under the Purchase and Sale Agreement: whether to object to zoning matters before
the Inspection Period and Title/Survey objection deadline of July 18, 2025 (PSA §§
7.2(a), 8.3(a)); whether to require cure as a condition of Closing; and what must be
produced at Closing under PSA § 10.3(g), which obliges the Seller to deliver evidence
satisfactory to the Buyer and its counsel that all conditions of every land use approval
have been satisfied and that those approvals remain in full force and effect.
We have not been asked to opine on market value, environmental liability, or title.
Where our analysis touches on those matters it is only to the extent they bear on land
use compliance.

Our method was as follows, in this order:

4. Critical Issues
Each of the six issues below defeats the Report's conclusion in whole or in part. Each
requires a variance, an approval, or a cure that is not presently in hand. Because the
Inspection Period closes on July 18, 2025 and Closing is set for August 15, 2025,
each must be resolved, or expressly priced and allocated, before the earlier date. We
note at the outset that the Report's Section I contains the unqualified statement that
"No other variances, waivers, or exceptions are required for the existing
improvements and uses on the property as currently configured." That
statement is incorrect in respect of at least C-1, C-2, C-3 and C-6.

4.1 C-1 — Rear yard setback: a 7-foot deficiency on the north boundary,
certified as compliant
What the Report says. Section IV.A lists the B-3 minimum rear yard setback as "25
feet" with no qualification, and states that "The minimum rear yard setback in the B-3
district is 25 feet per § 245-18." Section IV.B records "Rear Yard — North (abutting
R-4) | 25 ft minimum | 28 ft (Building A) | COMPLIANT." Section IV.C concludes that
"The 28-foot rear yard setback exceeds the 25-foot minimum rear yard setback
required by § 245-18. This standard is met." Section IX.A repeats "Rear Yard Setback
— North (abutting R-4) | COMPLIANT."
What the record shows. Ordinance § 245-18(h)(3) provides that "The minimum rear
yard setback shall be twenty-five (25) feet. Where a rear yard abuts a residential
zone (R-1, R-2, R-3, R-4, or R-5), the minimum rear yard setback shall be
increased to thirty-five (35) feet." The summary table at § 245-18(j) states the
standard as "Rear Yard Setback — 25 feet (35 feet abutting residential zone)." The
Survey expressly records the applicable requirement as "35 ft min. (residential
buffer)" and the measured setback as 28.0 ft, and in Note 2 records that the north
boundary abuts Lots 5 and 6, Block 413, which are "classified R-4 Residential," that the
measured setback "is 7.0 feet less than the residential buffer requirement," and that
"No variance or other land use approval for this setback reduction was provided to the
surveyor."
Analysis. The Report had the predicate for the enhanced standard and applied it on
one boundary but not the other. Its own Section 3.3 states that the property abuts R-4
on the north and east and that "certain bulk standards in the B-3 district are enhanced
when a property abuts a residential zone." In Section IV.A the Report reproduces the
side yard enhancement faithfully — "15 feet (25 feet when abutting a residential zone)"
— while silently dropping the identical parenthetical from the rear yard line. This is not
a difference of planning judgment; it is a selective transcription of a parenthetical that
appears, in the same form, in both rows of the ordinance table. The consequence is a
7.0-foot shortfall (28.0 ft against 35.0 ft) that the Report certifies as compliance.
The Report also fails to engage the mechanism by which such a shortfall might be
lawfully excused. It does not mention § 245-55 at all. If the enhanced 35-foot rear yard


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                      Page 6 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



standard was not in effect when Building A was constructed in 2014, the building may
enjoy protection as a lawfully pre-existing nonconforming structure under § 245-55(a)
and N.J.S.A. 40:55D-68 — but the burden of establishing that status rests on the owner
under § 245-55(a), and § 245-55(d) would then bar any enlargement, extension,
reconstruction or structural alteration of Building A that does not conform. If the
standard was in effect in 2014, the building was constructed in violation of it and
requires a variance. On either branch of the analysis the Report's "COMPLIANT" is
wrong, and the Report never undertakes the inquiry that would distinguish the two.
We raise the dating of the standard as an open question at Section 10 (OQ-1).
A compounding problem. Section 245-18(h)(3) is not only a dimensional standard. It
further provides that "No portion of any building, structure, parking area,
loading area, or dumpster enclosure shall be located within the enhanced rear
yard setback when the rear yard abuts a residential zone, except for landscaping
and stormwater management facilities expressly approved by the Planning Board."
This clause is an outright prohibition rather than a setback to be measured, and
nonconforming-structure protection under § 245-55 does not reach it. The Survey and
the ESA both place the Building B loading dock and apron, and part of the rear parking
area, in the northern portion of the site directly abutting the R-4 boundary. That is
developed at H-2 and M-8.
Consequence. The property does not comply with § 245-18(h)(3) and holds no relief
from it. A bulk variance, or (if the standard post-dates 2014) a documented
nonconforming-structure determination, is required. Because the enhanced setback
also prohibits the parking and loading uses now conducted in the north yard, a
variance limited to the building line would not by itself cure the site.
Required action. Obtain (i) the zoning history confirming the effective date of the 35-
foot enhanced rear setback; (ii) a corrected setback analysis; and (iii) either a variance
application or a § 245-55 nonconforming determination, in each case addressing the
building, the loading area and the rear parking together.

4.2 C-2 — Warehouse/flex use occupies 30.58% of gross floor area against
a 25% ceiling
What the Report says. Section V.C(d) states that "The warehouse/flex use
represents approximately 24% of the total gross floor area on the site, which is within
the 25% maximum prescribed by § 245-15(c)(3)(d). This condition is satisfied." Section
V.C closes: "the warehouse/flex conditional use in Building B is in compliance with all
applicable conditions of § 245-15(c)(3)."
What the record shows. Section 245-15(c)(3)(d) provides that "The gross floor area
devoted to warehouse, distribution, or flex space use shall not exceed twenty-five
percent (25%) of the total gross floor area of all structures on the lot," with gross
floor area as defined in § 245-18(g). The inputs are not in dispute: Building B is 18,500
SF and total GFA on the lot is 60,500 SF (42,000 + 18,500), a figure the Report states
correctly in the same paragraph and which is confirmed by the Survey at Section 5.
Analysis. The quotient is 18,500 ÷ 60,500 = 30.58%, not 24%. Applying the ceiling
of 25% to total GFA of 60,500 SF gives a permitted warehouse/flex floor area of
15,125 SF; the existing 18,500 SF exceeds it by 3,375 SF. No computation on the
correct 60,500 SF base can produce 24%; a result near 24% requires a denominator of


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                    Page 7 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



approximately 77,000 SF, which has no support anywhere in the record. This is the
clearest arithmetic failure in the Report, and it is outcome-determinative: it converts a
conclusion of comfortable compliance into a 5.58 percentage-point violation of a
condition the Board must find satisfied before it can approve the use.
Consequence. The warehouse/flex use cannot be approved as configured. The
shortfall can be cured in one of three ways, each with different consequences: reduce
the warehouse/flex floor area in Building B to 15,125 SF or less; reallocate floor area
so that total GFA rises without increasing warehouse/flex area (for example by adding
a permitted use elsewhere, which would also need to satisfy the FAR, coverage and
parking standards); or obtain relief from the conditional use standard, which requires
a variance and is in any event discretionary. Standing alone this issue would prevent a
conditional use approval; combined with C-3 it means the use has no approval at all.
Required action. Recompute the ratio and require the Seller to identify the basis for
the 24% figure. Any cure should be modelled against the parking requirement, because
reducing warehouse area changes the § 245-42(b) parking calculation.

4.3 C-3 — No Planning Board conditional use approval for the
warehouse/flex use
What the Report says. Section V.C concludes: "No conditional use approval from the
Planning Board appears to be required beyond the conditions satisfied by the site as
currently configured." The Report's Section V.B nevertheless classifies the
warehouse/flex use correctly as a "Conditional Use" under § 245-15(c)(3).
What the record shows. Section 245-15(c) provides that conditional uses are
permitted "subject to approval by the Planning Board upon a finding that the
conditions specified herein and the general conditional use standards of § 245-22 are
satisfied," and that "The Planning Board may impose reasonable conditions upon any
conditional use approval." The variance resolution addresses the point twice and
without ambiguity. Paragraph 2(5) finds that the warehouse/flex use "is classified as a
conditional use ... and that the Applicant has indicated its intention to seek, or will be
required to obtain, separate conditional use approval from the Maplewood Planning
Board in connection with that use," and states that the variance relief "does not
constitute, and shall not be construed as, conditional use approval, site plan
approval, or any other form of land use approval other than the specific bulk variance
described herein." Condition 5 independently obliges the Applicant to obtain
"conditional use approval for the warehouse/flex use from the Maplewood Planning
Board." The Report itself lists the resolution among the documents reviewed and
summarises it at Section VI and Appendix B — but omits paragraph 2(5) and Condition
5 entirely.
Analysis. There are only three possibilities, and the Report reconciles none of them.
Either a conditional use approval exists and was not produced, or it does not exist and
the use has been operating since 2014 without the approval the ordinance requires, or
the Report's view that no approval is needed is correct — which would contradict both
§ 245-15(c) and the Board's express findings. The first is a document request; the
second is the most likely and is a live zoning violation; the third is not tenable. The
Report's closing sentence — that no conditional use approval "appears to be required"
— is an assertion of legal conclusion that the Report elsewhere disclaims the


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                    Page 8 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



competence to make (Section 2.3(2) states that the Report "does not constitute a legal
opinion").

4.4 C-4 — The variance is personal to the Seller and expires on transfer
What the Report says. Section VI states that "The Board's resolution memorializes
these conditions as binding obligations running with the variance approval. The
variance remains in effect and the property benefits from this approval."
Section I and Section IX.A each rely on the variance as the sole qualification to an
otherwise unqualified finding of compliance. Appendix B summarises the resolution as
granting "a reduced east side yard setback of 18 feet" and says nothing further. The
Report does not address transferability in relation to this variance and does not
mention the 90-day confirmation mechanism at all; its only reference to the subject is a
generic disclaimer in Section X that legal review of the "enforceability and
transferability of variance approvals" should be conducted by counsel.
What the record shows. Section 4 of the resolution provides that the variance "is
personal to the Applicant, Maplewood Gateway Associates LP, and its principals,"
and that it "shall expire automatically upon the occurrence of" either "(a) the approved
use is discontinued for a period of twelve (12) consecutive months" or "(b) the
property is transferred, conveyed, assigned, or otherwise alienated to any
person or entity other than the Applicant ... UNLESS the successor owner,
transferee, or assignee files an application with this Board for confirmation of
the variance within ninety (90) days of the date of transfer." It continues:
"Failure to file such application within the ninety (90) day period shall result in the
automatic expiration of this variance, and the property shall thereafter be required
to comply with the full setback requirements of § 245-18." The Board also "reserves the
right, upon any such confirmation application, to impose additional or modified
conditions." The Survey flags the point twice — in the surveyor's note at Section 1 and
again at Section 10.1(8) — and expressly declines to opine on it.
Analysis. The sale to Crescent Boulevard Holdings LLC is a transfer within limb (b).
On Closing the variance expires by its own terms unless the Buyer files a confirmation
application within 90 days, and even then the Board may impose additional or modified
conditions. Two points follow. First, the Report's phrase "binding obligations running
with the variance approval" glosses the distinction that matters: under § 245-58(b) the


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                    Page 9 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



conditions bind successors and assigns, but under § 4 of the resolution the variance
itself does not run with the land. Second, without the variance the east side yard
setback of 19.0 ft (Survey, Section 4) stands against the enhanced 25-foot requirement
of § 245-18(h)(2) — a 6.0-foot deficiency with no relief of any kind.
The practical consequence is larger than the setback itself. Without the variance,
Building B becomes at best a nonconforming structure under § 245-55(d), which may
be "maintained and repaired but shall not be enlarged, extended, reconstructed, or
structurally altered" unless the work conforms to current requirements. That would
sterilise the very expansion the Report promotes. Section IX.B(2) of the Report tells
the Buyer that the FAR of 0.3307 against a 1.50 maximum indicates "significant
remaining development capacity" and that "Any future expansion or development
would have considerable room within the existing FAR limitations." That advice is
materially incomplete: the binding constraint on expansion is not FAR but the east side
yard, and the relief that makes the east side yard tolerable lapses on Closing.
Consequence. The property's only dimensional relief is time-limited and conditional
on action by the Buyer after Closing. If the confirmation application is not filed by
roughly November 13, 2025 (90 days from an August 15, 2025 Closing), the variance
expires automatically and cannot be revived by the Buyer without a fresh application.
Both the east setback and Building B's development potential are at stake.
Required action. Make the variance's survival a Closing condition. The Seller should
either procure a fresh variance that runs with the land, or join with the Buyer in a
confirmation application to the Board under § 4, with the Buyer participating so as to
be heard on any additional conditions. The Buyer should also calendar the 90-day
deadline on the day of Closing, and consider whether the PSA's 24-month survival
period for the § 5.3 zoning representations (PSA § 5.7) is long enough to reach a lapsed
variance.

What the Report says. Section IV.B records "Landscaped Buffer — East | Required
per variance condition | Landscape buffer exists along the eastern boundary |
COMPLIANT." Section IV.C states that "A landscape buffer is maintained along the
eastern property boundary in accordance with this condition." Section VI,
addressing compliance with Condition 1, states that "a landscape buffer is maintained
along the eastern property boundary in accordance with this condition." Section IX.A
records "Landscape Buffer — East | COMPLIANT."
What the record shows. Condition 1 of the resolution requires a "fifteen (15) foot
wide evergreen landscape buffer along the entire eastern property boundary,"
consisting of "a minimum of one (1) evergreen tree per eight (8) linear feet of
boundary, with a minimum planting height of six (6) feet at the time of installation,
supplemented by evergreen shrubs planted in staggered rows to create a continuous
visual screen achieving a minimum opacity of seventy-five percent (75%) within two (2)
growing seasons," on a landscape plan prepared by a licensed landscape architect and
"submitted to the Borough Zoning Officer for review and approval prior to the issuance
of a Certificate of Occupancy for Building B." Section 245-18(i) independently requires
a 15-foot buffer planted with a mix of evergreen trees and shrubs sufficient to provide
year-round screening to a minimum height of six feet within three years.


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                   Page 10 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



The Survey, at Section 7, measured the buffer at three cross-sections: 11.8 ft at the
north end, 12.2 ft at the midpoint and 12.0 ft at the south end, for an average of
12.0 ft. It records that the plantings are "sparse deciduous trees and shrubs,
predominantly maple (Acer spp.) and ornamental cherry (Prunus spp.)," that "No
evergreen species were identified along the buffer at the time of the field survey,"
that there was "No continuous ground cover planting," and that "No fencing was
observed." The surveyor notes that the measured width is "3.0 feet less than the
required 15.0 feet" and that the plantings are "predominantly deciduous rather than
evergreen." The ESA, at Section 4, independently recorded a buffer "approximately 12
feet in width, consisting primarily of deciduous shrubs." (It did so expressly without
addressing zoning compliance, as it was entitled to do.)

evidence: width (12.0 ft against 15.0 ft, a 20% shortfall sustained across all three
cross-sections and not attributable to a single narrow point); composition (no
evergreen species at all, where evergreens are the specified and only acceptable
means of achieving year-round screening); and continuous screen (sparse plantings,
no continuous ground cover, opacity untested but plainly not 75%). A fourth element —
whether the licensed landscape architect's plan was approved by the Zoning Officer
before the Building B certificate of occupancy issued — cannot be tested on the record
before us and is carried as a document request.
The Report's method is the source of the error. It did not measure the buffer; it did not
commission a measurement; and it conducted no site visit (Section 2.3(5) of the Report
confirms this). It asserted compliance from the existence of vegetation. The Survey,
which the Report relies on for every other dimension in the document, contains the
contradictory measurement in a section the Report does not cite.

provides that a violation of "any condition of a variance approval" is subject to the
penalties established by N.J.S.A. 40:55D-18, with each day after a notice to cure
constituting a separate offence. More importantly for the transaction, the buffer is the
consideration on which the Board's findings rest. Finding 2 of the resolution grants
relief "provided that adequate buffering and screening is installed along the entire
eastern boundary" and finds that "the conditions imposed herein will adequately
protect" the neighbouring residents. A deficient buffer therefore does two things at
once: it is an enforceable violation, and it supplies the Board with a ready basis to
impose additional or modified conditions on the § 4 confirmation application — a live
risk given C-4.
Required action. Either restore the buffer to Condition 1 (15.0 ft clear width, one
evergreen per 8 linear feet at 6 ft minimum installation height, staggered evergreen
shrubs to 75% opacity) with Zoning Officer sign-off, or obtain a modification of
Condition 1 from the Board. Restoration should be costed as part of the cure package,
since the eastern boundary also carries the 19-foot building setback that limits any re-
grading.

5.1 H-1 — There is no landscape buffer at all along the north boundary
What the Report says. Section IV.A correctly states the rule: "The 15-foot landscape
buffer requirement applies along any property boundary that abuts a residential
zone, independent of the setback standards." Having stated it correctly, the Report

("Landscaped Buffer — East"); Section IV.C discusses the east buffer alone; Section VI
addresses Condition 1 of the variance, which is also east-only.
What the record shows. Section 245-18(i) requires that where a lot in the B-3
district abuts a residential zone, "a landscaped buffer strip not less than fifteen (15)
feet in width shall be provided along the entire length of the property line
abutting the residential zone," and that "The buffer area shall not contain any

extending into the northeast corner.

boundaries that engage it. The omission is not formal: the north buffer zone is
occupied by the three uses § 245-18(i) expressly excludes from a buffer — a loading
area, a driveway and parking — so the requirement is not merely unfulfilled but
affirmatively defeated.
Consequence. A distinct violation of § 245-18(i) on the north boundary, additional to
the east-buffer violation at C-5 and the rear setback violation at C-1. The three issues
share a physical solution on the north boundary and should be designed and costed
together.

abutting R-4, and a landscape plan that reconciles the buffer with the loading,
driveway and parking areas now occupying it.

5.2 H-2 — The loading dock and apron are wholly unscreened and sit in a
yard where loading is prohibited
What the Report says. Section V.C(b), addressing conditional use condition (b) on
screening, contains no analysis of screening at all. It states only that "The site layout
provides for loading activity associated with the warehouse/flex use in Building B.
Loading access is facilitated by the existing curb cuts and internal circulation drives.
The site plan accommodates the operational needs of the warehouse/flex use within
the overall site design." The Report then certifies condition (b) satisfied as part of its
blanket conclusion that the use complies with "all applicable conditions of § 245-15(c)
(3)."
What the record shows. Section 245-15(c)(3)(b) requires that "All truck loading
areas, loading docks, and service areas shall be screened from adjacent residential
zones by a solid fence or wall not less than six (6) feet in height supplemented
by evergreen plantings, such that the loading operations are not visible from any
residential property or residential zone boundary," and that the screening "shall be
installed prior to the commencement of the warehouse, distribution, or flex space
use and shall be perpetually maintained." Section 245-42(g)(5) imposes a parallel
requirement, and adds that "Where a loading area is located within one hundred (100)
feet of a residential zone boundary, the screening requirement shall apply regardless
of intervening topography, structures, or vegetation." Section 245-18(h)(3)
prohibits loading areas within the enhanced rear yard altogether.
The Survey records, at Sections 3.2 and 6, "One at-grade loading dock and apron
area ... on the north side of Building B, facing the rear (north) property boundary and
the R-4 Residential zone. The loading dock apron area measures approximately 40 feet
by 25 feet. No screening wall, fence, or landscape screening structures were
observed surrounding or adjacent to the loading dock area at the time of the field
survey." The conditional use was commenced in 2014; the screening, if it ever existed,
was required to be installed before commencement.
Analysis. This is a failure to analyse a mandatory condition, presented as a finding
that the condition is satisfied. Four separate requirements fail on the field evidence:
the 6-foot solid fence or wall (absent); the evergreen supplement (absent); the pre-
commencement installation (cannot have occurred, since nothing is there); and the
perpetual maintenance obligation. Separately, the apron is 25 feet deep and abuts the
residential boundary directly, so it is unquestionably within 100 feet of the R-4 zone
and within the enhanced rear yard. Because condition (b) is a condition that the
Planning Board must find satisfied before approving the conditional use, this issue
independently defeats the conditional use in its present configuration and compounds
C-3.
We note a conflict in the record on orientation that should be resolved before any
application is prepared: the Survey places the dock on the north side of Building B,
while the ESA, at Section 4, records "A loading dock was observed on the west side of
Building B." The distinction is not academic — it determines which yard and which
enhanced standard apply, and whether the loading area is prohibited outright under §
245-18(h)(3). This is carried as open question OQ-3.
Consequence. Breach of § 245-15(c)(3)(b), § 245-42(g)(5) and § 245-18(h)(3). Cure
requires either a 6-foot masonry wall or solid fence supplemented with evergreens, or


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                   Page 14 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



relocation of the loading function — the latter being constrained by the rear and east
setbacks.
Required action. Include in the cure package: a screening design meeting § 245-
15(c)(3)(b) and § 245-42(g)(5), a verification of the dock's true orientation, and a
variance addressing any loading area that remains within the enhanced rear yard.

5.3 H-3 — Off-street loading was never analysed; the site provides one
space against five required
What the Report says. Nothing. Section VII is titled "Off-Street Parking Compliance"
and addresses parking ratios only. Section 245-42 is titled "Off-Street Parking and
Loading Requirements," and the Report cites it as the governing provision without
addressing its loading subsections. Loading appears in the Report only as a descriptive
phrase in Section V.C(b) ("Loading access is facilitated by the existing curb cuts").
What the record shows. Section 245-42(g)(1) requires at least one off-street loading
space for any commercial, industrial or warehouse use exceeding 10,000 SF of gross
floor area; subsection (2) requires "one (1) additional loading space ... for each
additional twenty-five thousand (25,000) square feet of gross floor area or fraction
thereof." Applied to the two buildings: Building A (42,000 SF commercial) requires 1 +
2 = 3 spaces; Building B (18,500 SF warehouse) requires 1 + 1 = 2 spaces; five
spaces in total. The Survey identifies one loading dock and apron on the site.
Analysis. On the Report's own floor areas the site is short by four loading spaces. Two
caveats should be stated rather than assumed. First, § 245-42(g) does not expressly
state whether the calculation is performed per building or for the lot as a whole; the
per-building reading is the more natural, since subsections (1) and (2) are framed by
reference to the use and its floor area, and it is the reading that produces five. Even on
a lot-wide reading the requirement would be 1 + 2 = 3 spaces, and the site would still
be short. Second, subsection (3) requires each loading space to have minimum
dimensions of 12 ft in width, 40 ft in length and 14 ft of vertical clearance; the apron
measures 40 × 25 ft and the overhead door is 12 × 14 ft, so even the single existing
space appears unable to accommodate a 40-foot length together with the on-site
manoeuvring that subsection (6) requires to be kept off the public right-of-way.
Consequence. A deficiency under a provision the ordinance ties to occupancy: the
preamble to § 245-42 provides that "No certificate of occupancy shall be issued, and no
use shall be commenced, changed, or expanded, unless the parking and loading
requirements of this section are satisfied or a variance therefrom has been granted."
Physically providing five compliant loading spaces on this site will be difficult given the
R-4 abutments on the north and east; a loading variance may be the only realistic
route, which should be identified now rather than after Closing.
Required action. Add a loading analysis to the Report; count and dimension every
existing loading space; and include a loading variance in the cure package if the
deficiency cannot be designed out.

What the record shows. Section 245-50(c)(2)(i): "Each building shall be permitted a
maximum of two (2) wall signs. For the purposes of this subsection, each physically
separate building on a lot shall be considered individually." The Survey confirms
"Three (3) wall-mounted tenant identification signs were observed on the
Crescent Boulevard (south) facade of Building A, each approximately 20 square feet in
area."
Analysis. The Report tested the area limit and not the numerical limit. Its conclusion
is carefully worded to be true and incomplete — signage is "within the maximum
allowable area" — while the count exceeds the limit by one. The aggregate area is
comfortably compliant (60 SF against 120 linear feet × 1.5 SF/LF = 180 SF), and no
individual sign approaches the 60 SF cap in § 245-50(c)(2)(iii); the failure is exclusively
one of count.
Consequence. One sign must be removed, consolidated, or covered by a variance.
The practical complexity is that tenant identification signs are commonly granted to
tenants as lease rights, so removal may require a lease review and tenant consent; we
recommend that the rent roll and leases be reviewed before the remedy is selected.
Required action. Review leases for signage rights; obtain removal or consolidation of
one sign, or a sign variance; and correct the signage certification to test count, area,
illumination, projection, and the roofline and edge limits in § 245-50(c)(2)(iv)–(vi).

5.5 H-5 — Uses were never verified at tenant level, and the fitness studio
appears to be a prohibited use
What the Report says. Section V.B lists four uses — retail, professional office,
mixed-use structure, and warehouse/flex — and certifies each compliant. Section
II.2.3(4) confirms that "No interior inspection of buildings on the property was
conducted," and Section 2.1 confines the scope by stating that "No operational audit of
tenant activities or business practices was conducted." The use analysis therefore rests
on Certificate of Occupancy records that the Report cites but does not identify.
What the record shows. The ESA, at Section 4, records that "Retail tenants
occupying ground-floor spaces at the time of the reconnaissance included a fitness
studio, a coffee shop, and an insurance office." Section 245-15(a) enumerates the
permitted principal uses in B-3: retail sales establishments; professional and business
offices; personal service establishments ("barber shops, hair salons, beauty parlors,
dry cleaning and laundry pick-up establishments ..., tailors, and shoe repair shops");
banks and financial institutions; restaurants, "subject to site plan approval by the
Planning Board pursuant to § 245-30"; mixed-use structures; public and quasi-public
uses; and parking structures. Section 245-15(d)(7) provides that "Any use not
expressly listed as a permitted principal use, permitted accessory use, or conditional
use in this section shall be deemed prohibited."
Analysis. A fitness studio does not appear in § 245-15(a). It is not readily
characterised as "retail sales" (no goods are sold), it is not one of the enumerated
"personal service establishments" (every listed example is a grooming or garment-care
service), and it is not a professional or business office. On the plain text of § 245-15(d)

(7) it is a prohibited use in the B-3 district unless the ordinance has been amended or a
use variance has been obtained — and the Report, which never identified the tenant,
could not have considered either possibility. The coffee shop engages a different
requirement: as a "restaurant" within § 245-15(a)(5) it required site plan approval by
the Planning Board, which the Report does not verify.
The use classification also affects the parking calculation, which the Report treats as
settled. The retail ratio of 1 space per 250 SF was applied to the whole 14,000 SF
ground floor. A fitness use is not listed in § 245-42(b); under the proviso to that
subsection the Zoning Officer must determine its requirement "based on the most
similar listed use," subject to appeal to the Zoning Board. If the fitness studio occupies
a material share of the ground floor, the 169-space requirement the Report computes
may not be the applicable requirement.
Consequence. A possible prohibited use together with a possible unapproved
restaurant use, in each case capable of enforcement under § 245-62, and an unsound
basis for the parking computation. This is a document-production issue as much as an
analytical one: it can be resolved by obtaining the rent roll and tenant schedule.
Required action. Obtain the rent roll and a tenant-by-tenant schedule of use and
floor area; obtain the zoning permits and certificates of occupancy for each tenancy
under § 245-60; and reconfirm the parking computation against actual uses.

5.6 H-6 — The Buyer has no right to rely on the Report, and the Report
ignores the ESA's recognised environmental condition
This issue has three limbs, and they point in the same direction: the Buyer's real
protection must come from the Seller's contractual representations and from a Buyer-
commissioned review, not from the Report.
(a) Reliance. The Report's Confidentiality Notice provides that it has been "prepared
for the exclusive use of Maplewood Gateway Associates LP" and that Pinnacle
"assumes no responsibility to any third party who may rely on this report." Section X is
more explicit: the Report "is prepared for the sole use and benefit of Maplewood
Gateway Associates LP and is not intended for reliance by any third party,
including but not limited to any prospective purchaser, lender, tenant, or
investor." Yet PSA § 5.3(e) delivers the Report to the Buyer as a due diligence
deliverable while stating that "Seller makes no independent representation as to the
accuracy, completeness, or currency of the Zoning Report." The result is that the
Buyer holds a document that is wrong in at least six material respects, which it has no
legal right to rely upon, and for which the Seller disclaims responsibility.
(b) Inverted reliance on the Survey. The Report derives every dimension it uses
from the Survey (Section 2.3(1) and Appendix A). But the Survey is certified to
Crescent Boulevard Holdings LLC, Ridgeline Title & Escrow, Briarcliff National Bank
and Holloway Stern LLP, and states that it "may not be relied upon by any other party
without the prior written consent of Cartwright Surveying Associates." The Seller's
consultant has therefore relied on an instrument it is not on its face entitled to rely
upon, while producing a report the Buyer is not entitled to rely upon. Neither
document is presently usable by both parties.
(c) The environmental condition. Section V.C(c) of the Report states that "we are
not aware of any hazardous materials being stored on the property in connection with


Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                   Page 17 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



the warehouse/flex use" and that "this condition is considered satisfied based on
available records." The ESA identifies REC-1: tetrachloroethylene from the former dry
cleaning operation at 1881 Crescent Boulevard (approximately 1978–2009), listed on
the NJDEP Known Contaminated Sites list under Program Interest No. 007624 with a
status of "Pending"; documented groundwater flow "generally east-northeast — that is,
from the contamination source toward the subject property"; monitoring wells
observed within 15 to 20 feet of the shared boundary; and a recommendation for a
Phase II including sub-slab soil vapour sampling beneath both buildings. The Report
does not list the ESA among the documents it reviewed (Section II.2.2).
We should be precise about what this does and does not establish. Section 245-15(c)(3)
(c) prohibits the storage of hazardous materials on the premises; contamination
migrating from an adjoining property is not "storage," so the conditional use condition
is not necessarily breached. The defect in the Report is different and still material: it
pronounced the condition satisfied "based on available records" without having the one
record that bears on it, and without acknowledging that the property may be affected
by a contaminant plume migrating toward it. A conclusion of compliance that is
reached without the governing environmental report is not a conclusion the Buyer
should accept, particularly where the Report is the Buyer's only zoning work product.
The separate and distinct failure to address the annual certification required by the
same subsection is at M-10.
Consequence. The Report cannot be the basis of the Buyer's decision. Either the
reliance defects are cured, or the Buyer must commission its own zoning review and
rest on the PSA representations.
Required action. Obtain (i) a reliance letter from Pinnacle Land Advisors Inc.
running to the Buyer, its counsel and its lender; (ii) a recertification of the Survey, or
the surveyor's written consent to reliance by the Seller and Pinnacle; and (iii) a Buyer-
commissioned zoning and land use review that integrates the ESA findings. Do not
treat the Report as a Seller representation.

6. Moderate-Severity Issues
The issues below either leave a requirement unverified or rest on an analytical basis
that is unsound or unsupported. None is presently established as a violation on the
documents in the record; several would convert to High or Critical once the municipal
file is produced. They should be closed out during the Inspection Period.

6.1 M-1 — Bicycle parking was never addressed
Finding. Section 245-42(d) requires that "All mixed-use developments and all
commercial developments providing fifty (50) or more vehicular parking spaces shall
provide bicycle parking at a ratio of one (1) bicycle parking space per twenty (20)
vehicular parking spaces, with a minimum of four (4) bicycle spaces," with racks that
support the frame upright, located within 100 feet of the main building entrance and
identified by signage. Applying the 187 spaces counted by the Survey gives 9.35,
rounded to 10 spaces. The Report does not mention bicycle parking, and the Survey
does not identify any racks. This is a mandatory standard in the same section the
Report cites, and the property is both a mixed-use development and a commercial
development with more than 50 spaces, so the requirement is engaged twice over.
Action. Confirm whether bicycle parking exists; if not, install 10 spaces within 100
feet of the Building A main entrance with signage, or include the deficiency in the cure
package and the Report correction.

6.2 M-2 — Accessible parking: the count is adequate, the specification is
unverified
Finding. Section 245-42(e) requires, for a lot with 151 to 200 spaces, a minimum of 6
accessible spaces including 1 van-accessible space; van-accessible spaces must be
at least 11 feet wide with an adjacent 5-foot access aisle, and accessible spaces must
be on the shortest accessible route to the entrance. The Survey counts "8 ADA-
accessible spaces located near the main entrance to Building A," so the numerical
requirement is met with a margin. The Report asserts compliance generically —
"Accessible parking spaces are provided in accordance with the Americans with
Disabilities Act and the New Jersey Barrier Free Subcode, as reflected in the building
permit records" — without recording the width, aisle, signage or route of any space.
Action. Obtain a striping and signage plan or an accessibility survey confirming at
least one van-accessible space of the specified dimensions.

6.3 M-3 — The 28-foot rear-yard figure cannot be reconciled with the
survey's own geometry
Finding. The Survey attributes the 28.0-foot rear yard to Building A, "measured ...
from the north face of Building A to the north property line," and the Report adopts
that attribution. The geometry does not close. Building A has a 14,000 SF footprint; the
Report gives its Crescent Boulevard frontage as approximately 120 linear feet, which
implies a depth of about 116.7 feet. The Report and the Survey both give the front yard
as 22.0 feet and the lot depth as 587.0 feet. On those figures Building A's north face
stands roughly 139 feet from the Crescent Boulevard line and roughly 448 feet from
the north property line — not 28 feet.



Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | May 6, 2025                                   Page 20 of 37
       Holloway Stern LLP | Zoning Issues Memorandum | 1875 Crescent Boulevard, Block 412, Lot 17, Maplewood, NJ



The 28.0-foot measurement is far more plausibly a measurement of Building B, which
the Survey places "in the northern portion of the site, behind and to the north of
Building A." If that is so, Building B's north face is 28 feet from the R-4 boundary and
its 25-foot-deep loading apron extends to within about 3 feet of it. That would place the
entire loading operation inside the 35-foot enhanced rear setback, and directly
opposite R-4 residences across the boundary — which is consistent with H-2 and gives
that issue a larger footprint than the Report suggests.
This does not soften C-1. Whichever building stands 28 feet from the north line, the
measured setback is 7 feet short of the 35-foot requirement. What it changes is which
structure requires relief, and how much of the site is affected. It also means the
Report's statement that "The rear yard setback of 28 feet for Building A exceeds the
applicable 25-foot minimum" describes a condition that cannot exist on the survey's
own dimensions.
Action. Obtain a corrected setback exhibit from Cartwright Surveying Associates
identifying the rear setback for each building separately, together with the dimension
from each building to the nearest point of the north property line.

6.4 M-4 — The character of the north yard is unresolved, and it affects the
standard applied
Finding. The Survey's boundary description at Section 2 states that the property is
bounded "on the north by Lots 5 and 6, Block 413 (R-4 Residential zone)" and
identifies no street along that line; the metes and bounds description runs the north
line between the northeast and northwest corners without reference to Elm Terrace.
But Sections 6 and 9 of the same Survey identify Elm Terrace, a 40-foot publicly
dedicated right-of-way, at the rear of the site, with Curb Cut No. 3 taken from it at the
northwest corner. The Report follows neither description consistently: Section 3.3 says
the property has "frontage on both Crescent Boulevard to the south and Elm Terrace to
the north (rear)," while Section IV.C says the north boundary "adjoins Elm Terrace,
beyond which lies the R-4 Residential District."

Finding. The Survey's boundary description at Section 2 states that the property is
bounded "on the north by Lots 5 and 6, Block 413 (R-4 Residential zone)" and
identifies no street along that line; the metes and bounds description runs the north
line between the northeast and northwest corners without reference to Elm Terrace.
But Sections 6 and 9 of the same Survey identify Elm Terrace, a 40-foot publicly
dedicated right-of-way, at the rear of the site, with Curb Cut No. 3 taken from it at the
northwest corner. The Report follows neither description consistently: Section 3.3 says
the property has "frontage on both Crescent Boulevard to the south and Elm Terrace to
the north (rear)," while Section IV.C says the north boundary "adjoins Elm Terrace,
beyond which lies the R-4 Residential District."
Two characterisations are available, and they produce different obligations. If the
north yard is a rear yard abutting a residential zone, the 35-foot enhanced setback
and the prohibition on parking, loading and structures within it both apply (C-1), as
does the 15-foot buffer (H-1). If the north line is a street frontage on Elm Terrace,
then the 20-foot front yard standard in § 245-18(h)(1) applies — that subsection
provides that on a corner lot each street frontage is deemed a front yard, and a lot with
frontage on two streets presents the analogous question — and § 245-42(g)(4) prohibits
loading spaces "within any required front yard setback area." Whichever
characterisation is correct, the loading area in the north yard fails; but the relief
required differs, and the buffer obligation may differ as well.
Action. Request a written determination from the Zoning Officer on the character of
the north yard. This is the single cheapest step available to fix the applicable standard,
and it should precede any application.

Finding. Beyond height and area (C-6), § 245-50 imposes further requirements on a
B-3 monument sign, none of which the Report addresses: a minimum 5-foot setback

architectural precast concrete, with wood and unfinished concrete block prohibited (§
245-50(c)(1)(v)); and illumination only by shielded external fixtures or reverse-channel
letters with an opaque cabinet (§ 245-50(c)(1)(vi)). The Survey places the sign
"immediately east of the primary curb cut (Curb Cut No. 1)," which makes the sight-
